parts.prompt_html:
Use standard summation formulae to simplify

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\left(3 r + 2\right) \left(3 r + 8\right)\right)\]

in terms of \(n\).
parts.solution_html:
Expand the summand and separate its powers of \(r\).

\[\left(3 r + 2\right) \left(3 r + 8\right)=9 r^{2} + 30 r + 16\]

Use the standard formulae; the constant is counted once for each of the \(n\) terms.

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\left(3 r + 2\right) \left(3 r + 8\right)\right)=9\left(\frac{n \left(n + 1\right) \left(2 n + 1\right)}{6}\right)+30\left(\frac{n \left(n + 1\right)}{2}\right)+16\left(n\right)\]
\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\left(3 r + 2\right) \left(3 r + 8\right)\right)=\frac{n \left(6 n^{2} + 39 n + 65\right)}{2}\]
parts.hint_html: Expand before applying the standard summation formulae.

marking_points.criterion_html: Expand and separate the polynomial into standard sums.
Apply the summation formulae with the correct limits and number of constant terms.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html:
Use the method of differences to find

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\frac{1}{\left(3 r + 2\right) \left(3 r + 8\right)}\right)\]

in terms of \(n\).
parts.solution_html:
Use the following difference, obtained by combining the terms over a common denominator:

\[\frac{1}{\left(3 r + 2\right) \left(3 r + 8\right)}=\frac{1}{6 \left(3 r + 2\right)}-\left(\frac{1}{6 \left(3 r + 8\right)}\right)\]

Writing \(F(r)=\frac{1}{6 \left(3 r + 2\right)}\) and denoting the requested finite sum by \(S_n\), the cancellation is

\[\begin{aligned}S_n&=[F(1)-F(3)]\\&\quad+[F(2)-F(4)]+\cdots\\&\quad+[F(n)-F(n + 2)].\end{aligned}\]

Only the first 2 and last 2 boundary terms remain (the formula also covers overlapping boundaries).

\[S_n=\frac{1}{30}+\frac{1}{48}-\left(\frac{1}{6 \left(3 n + 5\right)}\right)-\left(\frac{1}{6 \left(3 n + 8\right)}\right)\]
\[S_n=\frac{n \left(39 n + 89\right)}{80 \left(3 n + 5\right) \left(3 n + 8\right)}\]
parts.hint_html: Find a difference F(r)−F(r+h), then write the boundary terms before simplifying.

marking_points.criterion_html: Find an appropriate partial-fraction or difference representation.
Obtain the correct coefficients in that representation.
Display cancellation and retain every required boundary term.

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Determine whether the corresponding infinite series converges and, if it does, find its sum.
parts.solution_html:
The partial sums satisfy

\[S_n=\frac{n \left(39 n + 89\right)}{80 \left(3 n + 5\right) \left(3 n + 8\right)}\]

Taking the limit as \(n\to\infty\) gives a finite number:

\[\lim_{n\to\infty}S_n=\frac{13}{240}\]

Therefore the series converges to this value.
parts.hint_html: Use the finite partial sum, not a sum of separate divergent series.
parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html:
Use standard summation formulae to simplify

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\left(2 r - 1\right) \left(2 r + 3\right)\right)\]

in terms of \(n\).
parts.solution_html:
Expand the summand and separate its powers of \(r\).

\[\left(2 r - 1\right) \left(2 r + 3\right)=4 r^{2} + 4 r - 3\]

Use the standard formulae; the constant is counted once for each of the \(n\) terms.

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\left(2 r - 1\right) \left(2 r + 3\right)\right)=4\left(\frac{n \left(n + 1\right) \left(2 n + 1\right)}{6}\right)+4\left(\frac{n \left(n + 1\right)}{2}\right)-3\left(n\right)\]
\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\left(2 r - 1\right) \left(2 r + 3\right)\right)=\frac{n \left(4 n^{2} + 12 n - 1\right)}{3}\]

\[\frac{1}{\left(2 r - 1\right) \left(2 r + 3\right)}=\frac{1}{4 \left(2 r - 1\right)}-\left(\frac{1}{4 \left(2 r + 3\right)}\right)\]

Writing \(F(r)=\frac{1}{4 \left(2 r - 1\right)}\) and denoting the requested finite sum by \(S_n\), the cancellation is

\[S_n=\frac{n \left(4 n + 5\right)}{3 \left(2 n + 1\right) \left(2 n + 3\right)}\]

parts.solution_html:
Each root satisfies \(z^4+4z^2-2z+5=0\). Sum over all four roots:

parts.prompt_html:
Find a simplified expression for

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left[(\alpha^2+2r-1)^2+(\beta^2+2r-1)^2+(\gamma^2+2r-1)^2+(\delta^2+2r-1)^2\right].\]
parts.solution_html:
Expand the four squares before summing in \(r\). Their total is

\[4(2r-1)^2+2(2r-1)P_2+P_4=16 r^{2} - 48 r + 32\]

Expand the summand and separate its powers of \(r\).

\[16 r^{2} - 48 r + 32=16 r^{2} - 48 r + 32\]

Use the standard formulae; the constant is counted once for each of the \(n\) terms.

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(16 r^{2} - 48 r + 32\right)=16\left(\frac{n \left(n + 1\right) \left(2 n + 1\right)}{6}\right)-48\left(\frac{n \left(n + 1\right)}{2}\right)+32\left(n\right)\]
\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(16 r^{2} - 48 r + 32\right)=\frac{16 n \left(n - 2\right) \left(n - 1\right)}{3}\]

parts.solution_html:

Writing \(F(r)=\frac{1}{r^{2} + 3 r + 3}\) and denoting the requested finite sum by \(S_n\), the cancellation is

Only the first 1 and last 1 boundary terms remain (the formula also covers overlapping boundaries).

\[S_n=\frac{1}{7}-\left(\frac{1}{3 n + \left(n + 1\right)^{2} + 6}\right)\]

parts.answer_html: \[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\frac{6 k}{\left(k + 3 r\right) \left(k + 3 r + 3\right)}\right)=\frac{6 k n}{\left(k + 3\right) \left(k + 3 n + 3\right)}\]
parts.solution_html:
Use the following difference, obtained by combining the terms over a common denominator:

\[\frac{6 k}{\left(k + 3 r\right) \left(k + 3 r + 3\right)}=\frac{2 k}{k + 3 r}-\left(\frac{2 k}{k + 3 r + 3}\right)\]

Writing \(F(r)=\frac{2 k}{k + 3 r}\) and denoting the requested finite sum by \(S_n\), the cancellation is

\[\begin{aligned}S_n&=[F(1)-F(2)]\\&\quad+[F(2)-F(3)]+\cdots\\&\quad+[F(n)-F(n + 1)].\end{aligned}\]

Only the first 1 and last 1 boundary terms remain (the formula also covers overlapping boundaries).

\[S_n=\frac{2 k}{k + 3}-\left(\frac{2 k}{k + 3 n + 3}\right)\]
\[S_n=\frac{6 k n}{\left(k + 3\right) \left(k + 3 n + 3\right)}\]

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\frac{3^{- r - 1} \left(2 r + 3\right)}{r \left(r + 1\right)}\right)\]

in terms of \(n\).
parts.answer_html:
\[\frac{2 r + 3}{r \left(r + 1\right)}=\frac{3}{r}-\frac{1}{r + 1}\]
\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\frac{3^{- r - 1} \left(2 r + 3\right)}{r \left(r + 1\right)}\right)=\frac{3^{- n} \left(3^{n} n + 3^{n} - 1\right)}{3 \left(n + 1\right)}\]
parts.solution_html:
First decompose the rational factor:

\[\frac{2 r + 3}{r \left(r + 1\right)}=\frac{3}{r}-\frac{1}{r + 1}\]

Use the following difference, obtained by combining the terms over a common denominator:

\[\frac{3^{- r - 1} \left(2 r + 3\right)}{r \left(r + 1\right)}=\frac{3^{- r}}{r}-\left(\frac{3^{- r - 1}}{r + 1}\right)\]

Writing \(F(r)=\frac{3^{- r}}{r}\) and denoting the requested finite sum by \(S_n\), the cancellation is

\[\begin{aligned}S_n&=[F(1)-F(2)]\\&\quad+[F(2)-F(3)]+\cdots\\&\quad+[F(n)-F(n + 1)].\end{aligned}\]

Only the first 1 and last 1 boundary terms remain (the formula also covers overlapping boundaries).

\[S_n=\frac{1}{3}-\left(\frac{3^{- n - 1}}{n + 1}\right)\]
\[S_n=\frac{3^{- n} \left(3^{n} n + 3^{n} - 1\right)}{3 \left(n + 1\right)}\]

parts.prompt_html:
Use the method of differences to find

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\frac{6 r^{2} + 12 r + 8}{r^{3} \left(r + 2\right)^{3}}\right)\]

in terms of \(n\).
parts.answer_html: \[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\frac{6 r^{2} + 12 r + 8}{r^{3} \left(r + 2\right)^{3}}\right)=\frac{n \left(9 n^{5} + 81 n^{4} + 297 n^{3} + 551 n^{2} + 522 n + 204\right)}{8 \left(n + 1\right)^{3} \left(n + 2\right)^{3}}\]
parts.solution_html:
Use the following difference, obtained by combining the terms over a common denominator:

\[\frac{6 r^{2} + 12 r + 8}{r^{3} \left(r + 2\right)^{3}}=\frac{1}{r^{3}}-\left(\frac{1}{\left(r + 2\right)^{3}}\right)\]

Writing \(F(r)=\frac{1}{r^{3}}\) and denoting the requested finite sum by \(S_n\), the cancellation is

\[\begin{aligned}S_n&=[F(1)-F(3)]\\&\quad+[F(2)-F(4)]+\cdots\\&\quad+[F(n)-F(n + 2)].\end{aligned}\]

Only the first 2 and last 2 boundary terms remain (the formula also covers overlapping boundaries).

\[S_n=1+\frac{1}{8}-\left(\frac{1}{\left(n + 1\right)^{3}}\right)-\left(\frac{1}{\left(n + 2\right)^{3}}\right)\]
\[S_n=\frac{n \left(9 n^{5} + 81 n^{4} + 297 n^{3} + 551 n^{2} + 522 n + 204\right)}{8 \left(n + 1\right)^{3} \left(n + 2\right)^{3}}\]
parts.hint_html: Find a difference F(r)−F(r+h), then write the boundary terms before simplifying.

marking_points.criterion_html: Find an appropriate partial-fraction or difference representation.
Obtain the correct coefficients in that representation.
Display cancellation and retain every required boundary term.

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Determine whether the corresponding infinite series converges and, if it does, find its sum.
parts.solution_html:
The partial sums satisfy

\[S_n=\frac{n \left(9 n^{5} + 81 n^{4} + 297 n^{3} + 551 n^{2} + 522 n + 204\right)}{8 \left(n + 1\right)^{3} \left(n + 2\right)^{3}}\]

Taking the limit as \(n\to\infty\) gives a finite number:

\[\lim_{n\to\infty}S_n=\frac{9}{8}\]

Therefore the series converges to this value.
parts.hint_html: Use the finite partial sum, not a sum of separate divergent series.

marking_points.criterion_html: Take the limit of the partial sum and justify the limiting boundary value(s).

parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: Find the cubic equation whose roots are \(u=2\alpha-1,\ v=2\beta-1,\ w=2\gamma-1\).
parts.solution_html:
Set \(y=2x-1\), so \(x=(y+1)/2\). Substituting into the original equation and simplifying gives

\[y^{3} + 2 y^{2} - y - 3=0.\]
parts.label: a

parts.solution_html:
From the transformed cubic, \(u+v+w=-2\) and \(uv+vw+wu=-1\). Thus

\[u^2+v^2+w^2=(-2)^2-2(-1)=6.\]
parts.hint_html: Use the first two coefficient relations.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html:
Find and simplify

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left[(r+u)^2+(r+v)^2+(r+w)^2\right].\]
parts.solution_html:
The expression in brackets is \(3 r^{2} - 4 r + 6\).

Expand the summand and separate its powers of \(r\).

\[3 r^{2} - 4 r + 6=3 r^{2} - 4 r + 6\]

Use the standard formulae; the constant is counted once for each of the \(n\) terms.

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(3 r^{2} - 4 r + 6\right)=3\left(\frac{n \left(n + 1\right) \left(2 n + 1\right)}{6}\right)-4\left(\frac{n \left(n + 1\right)}{2}\right)+6\left(n\right)\]
\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(3 r^{2} - 4 r + 6\right)=\frac{n \left(2 n^{2} - n + 9\right)}{2}\]
parts.hint_html: Expand in r and use the two root sums.
parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: Starting from \(r^2-(r-1)^2\), derive a formula for \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(2 r - 1\right)\).
parts.solution_html:
\[r^2-(r-1)^2=2r-1\]

Summing gives \(n^2-0^2=n^2\).
parts.hint_html: Use the consecutive squares from 0² to n².
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html:
Find \(a\) in terms of \(n\) if

\[\sum_{r=n+1}^{3n}(2r-1+a)=4n.\]
parts.solution_html:
By part (a), the odd-number contribution is \((3n)^2-n^2=8n^2\). There are \(2n\) copies of \(a\), so

\[8n^2+2na=4n,\qquad a=2-4n.\]
parts.hint_html: Subtract the partial sums at 3n and n; add the correct number of copies of a.

marking_points.criterion_html: Count \(2n\) terms and form the parameter equation.

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find the sum and the sum of squares of \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\).
parts.solution_html:
By the coefficient relations, \(Q_1=2\), \(E_2=5\).

\[Q_2=Q_1^2-2E_2=-6\]
parts.hint_html: Apply the root-coefficient relations before expanding any shifted expressions.

marking_points.criterion_html: Obtain the appropriate sum \(2\) and pairwise-product sum \(5\).

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html:
Obtain a simplified polynomial expression in \(n\) for

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left[(3 r - 2+\alpha)^2+(3 r - 2+\beta)^2+(3 r - 2+\gamma)^2\right].\]
parts.solution_html:
The sum of the three squares at a fixed index is

\[3(3 r - 2)^2+2(3 r - 2)Q_1+Q_2=27 r^{2} - 24 r - 2\]

Expand the summand and separate its powers of \(r\).

\[27 r^{2} - 24 r - 2=27 r^{2} - 24 r - 2\]

Use the standard formulae; the constant is counted once for each of the \(n\) terms.

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(27 r^{2} - 24 r - 2\right)=27\left(\frac{n \left(n + 1\right) \left(2 n + 1\right)}{6}\right)-24\left(\frac{n \left(n + 1\right)}{2}\right)-2\left(n\right)\]
\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(27 r^{2} - 24 r - 2\right)=\frac{n \left(18 n^{2} + 3 n - 19\right)}{2}\]
parts.hint_html: Combine the three squares before summing in r.

marking_points.criterion_html: Use the root sum and square sum correctly.

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\frac{1}{\left(k r + 3\right) \left(k r - k + 3\right)}\right)\) in terms of \(n\) and \(k\).
parts.solution_html:
Use the following difference, obtained by combining the terms over a common denominator:

\[\frac{1}{\left(k r + 3\right) \left(k r - k + 3\right)}=\frac{1}{k \left(k r - k + 3\right)}-\left(\frac{1}{k \left(k \left(r + 1\right) - k + 3\right)}\right)\]

Writing \(F(r)=\frac{1}{k \left(k r - k + 3\right)}\) and denoting the requested finite sum by \(S_n\), the cancellation is

\[\begin{aligned}S_n&=[F(1)-F(2)]\\&\quad+[F(2)-F(3)]+\cdots\\&\quad+[F(n)-F(n + 1)].\end{aligned}\]

Only the first 1 and last 1 boundary terms remain (the formula also covers overlapping boundaries).

\[S_n=\frac{1}{3 k}-\left(\frac{1}{k \left(k \left(n + 1\right) - k + 3\right)}\right)\]
\[S_n=\frac{n}{3 \left(k n + 3\right)}\]
parts.hint_html: Find a difference F(r)−F(r+h), then write the boundary terms before simplifying.

marking_points.criterion_html: Find an appropriate partial-fraction or difference representation.
Display cancellation and retain every required boundary term.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Determine whether the corresponding infinite series converges and, if it does, find its sum.
parts.solution_html:
The partial sums satisfy

\[S_n=\frac{n}{3 \left(k n + 3\right)}\]

Taking the limit as \(n\to\infty\) gives a finite number:

\[\lim_{n\to\infty}S_n=\frac{1}{3 k}\]

Therefore the series converges to this value.
parts.hint_html: Use the finite partial sum, not a sum of separate divergent series.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find \(\sum_{r=n}^{2 n + 1}\left(\frac{1}{\left(k r + 3\right) \left(k r - k + 3\right)}\right)\).
parts.answer_html: \[T_n=\frac{n + 2}{\left(k n - k + 3\right) \left(2 k n + k + 3\right)}\]
parts.solution_html:
Use the same boundary cancellation over the new range:

\[T_n=F(n)-F(2n+2)\]
\[T_n=\frac{n + 2}{\left(k n - k + 3\right) \left(2 k n + k + 3\right)}\]
parts.hint_html: The last negative boundary term has index 2n+2.
parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: Find the sum and the sum of squares of \(\alpha^{-1},\beta^{-1},\gamma^{-1}\).
parts.solution_html:
The original product is \(2\). For the reciprocal roots,

\[Q_1=\frac{\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha}{\alpha\beta\gamma}=-2,\quad E_2=\frac{\alpha+\beta+\gamma}{\alpha\beta\gamma}=- \frac{3}{2}.\]
\[Q_2=Q_1^2-2E_2=7\]
parts.hint_html: Apply the root-coefficient relations before expanding any shifted expressions.

marking_points.criterion_html: Obtain the appropriate sum \(-2\) and pairwise-product sum \(- \frac{3}{2}\).

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html:
Obtain a simplified polynomial expression in \(n\) for

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left[(r+\alpha^{-1})^2+(r+\beta^{-1})^2+(r+\gamma^{-1})^2\right].\]
parts.solution_html:
The sum of the three squares at a fixed index is

\[3(r)^2+2(r)Q_1+Q_2=3 r^{2} - 4 r + 7\]

Expand the summand and separate its powers of \(r\).

\[3 r^{2} - 4 r + 7=3 r^{2} - 4 r + 7\]

Use the standard formulae; the constant is counted once for each of the \(n\) terms.

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(3 r^{2} - 4 r + 7\right)=3\left(\frac{n \left(n + 1\right) \left(2 n + 1\right)}{6}\right)-4\left(\frac{n \left(n + 1\right)}{2}\right)+7\left(n\right)\]
\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(3 r^{2} - 4 r + 7\right)=\frac{n \left(2 n^{2} - n + 11\right)}{2}\]
parts.hint_html: Combine the three squares before summing in r.

marking_points.criterion_html: Use the root sum and square sum correctly.

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html:
Use the method of differences to find

\[\sum_{r=0}^{n - 1}\left(\frac{k \left(2 k r + k + 2\right)}{\left(k r + 1\right)^{2} \left(k r + k + 1\right)^{2}}\right)\]

in terms of \(n\).
parts.answer_html: \[\sum_{r=0}^{n - 1}\left(\frac{k \left(2 k r + k + 2\right)}{\left(k r + 1\right)^{2} \left(k r + k + 1\right)^{2}}\right)=\frac{k n \left(k n + 2\right)}{\left(k n + 1\right)^{2}}\]
parts.solution_html:
Use the following difference, obtained by combining the terms over a common denominator:

\[\frac{k \left(2 k r + k + 2\right)}{\left(k r + 1\right)^{2} \left(k r + k + 1\right)^{2}}=\frac{1}{\left(k r + 1\right)^{2}}-\left(\frac{1}{\left(k \left(r + 1\right) + 1\right)^{2}}\right)\]

Writing \(F(r)=\frac{1}{\left(k r + 1\right)^{2}}\) and denoting the requested finite sum by \(S_n\), the cancellation is

\[\begin{aligned}S_n&=[F(0)-F(1)]\\&\quad+[F(1)-F(2)]+\cdots\\&\quad+[F(n - 1)-F(n)].\end{aligned}\]

Only the first 1 and last 1 boundary terms remain (the formula also covers overlapping boundaries).

\[S_n=1-\left(\frac{1}{\left(k n + 1\right)^{2}}\right)\]
\[S_n=\frac{k n \left(k n + 2\right)}{\left(k n + 1\right)^{2}}\]
parts.hint_html: Find a difference F(r)−F(r+h), then write the boundary terms before simplifying.

marking_points.criterion_html: Find an appropriate partial-fraction or difference representation.
Display cancellation and retain every required boundary term.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Determine whether the corresponding infinite series converges and, if it does, find its sum.
parts.answer_html: \[\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{k \left(2 k r + k + 2\right)}{\left(k r + 1\right)^{2} \left(k r + k + 1\right)^{2}}\right)=1\]
parts.solution_html:
The partial sums satisfy

\[S_n=\frac{k n \left(k n + 2\right)}{\left(k n + 1\right)^{2}}\]

Taking the limit as \(n\to\infty\) gives a finite number:

\[\lim_{n\to\infty}S_n=1\]

Therefore the series converges to this value.
parts.hint_html: Use the finite partial sum, not a sum of separate divergent series.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find \(\sum_{r=n}^{n^{2}}\left(\frac{k \left(2 k r + k + 2\right)}{\left(k r + 1\right)^{2} \left(k r + k + 1\right)^{2}}\right)\) in terms of \(n\) and \(k\).
parts.answer_html: \[T_n=\frac{k \left(n^{2} - n + 1\right) \left(k n^{2} + k n + k + 2\right)}{\left(k n + 1\right)^{2} \left(k n^{2} + k + 1\right)^{2}}\]
parts.solution_html:
The difference representation is valid at every index, so

\[T_n=F(n)-F(n^2+1)\]
\[T_n=\frac{k \left(n^{2} - n + 1\right) \left(k n^{2} + k n + k + 2\right)}{\left(k n + 1\right)^{2} \left(k n^{2} + k + 1\right)^{2}}\]
parts.hint_html: Do not replace n²+1 by (n+1)².

marking_points.criterion_html: Obtain \(\frac{k \left(n^{2} - n + 1\right) \left(k n^{2} + k n + k + 2\right)}{\left(k n + 1\right)^{2} \left(k n^{2} + k + 1\right)^{2}}\).

parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html:
Use standard summation formulae to simplify

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(5 r^{2} + 10 r - 6\right)\]

in terms of \(n\).
parts.solution_html:
Expand the summand and separate its powers of \(r\).

\[5 r^{2} + 10 r - 6=5 r^{2} + 10 r - 6\]

Use the standard formulae; the constant is counted once for each of the \(n\) terms.

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(5 r^{2} + 10 r - 6\right)=5\left(\frac{n \left(n + 1\right) \left(2 n + 1\right)}{6}\right)+10\left(\frac{n \left(n + 1\right)}{2}\right)-6\left(n\right)\]
\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(5 r^{2} + 10 r - 6\right)=\frac{n \left(10 n^{2} + 45 n - 1\right)}{6}\]
parts.hint_html: Expand before applying the standard summation formulae.

marking_points.criterion_html: Expand and separate the polynomial into standard sums.
Apply the summation formulae with the correct limits and number of constant terms.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\frac{5 r^{2} + 10 r - 6}{r \left(r + 2\right)}\right)\) by polynomial division followed by the method of differences.
parts.solution_html:
\[\frac{5 r^{2} + 10 r - 6}{r \left(r + 2\right)}=5-3\left(\frac1r-\frac1{r+2}\right)\]

There are two uncancelled terms at each end:

\[T_n=5n-3\left(1+\frac12-\frac1{n+1}-\frac1{n+2}\right).\]
\[T_n=\frac{n \left(10 n^{2} + 21 n + 5\right)}{2 \left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 2\right)}\]
parts.hint_html: Separate the constant 5 before telescoping.

marking_points.criterion_html: Retain both boundary terms at each end.

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Hence find \(\sum_{r=n + 1}^{3 n}\left(\frac{5 r^{2} + 10 r - 6}{r \left(r + 2\right)}\right)\).
parts.answer_html: \[U_n=\frac{2 n \left(45 n^{4} + 180 n^{3} + 217 n^{2} + 84 n + 5\right)}{\left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 2\right) \left(3 n + 1\right) \left(3 n + 2\right)}\]
parts.solution_html:
Subtract \(T_n\) from \(T_{3n}\), or telescope over the required range.

\[U_n=\frac{2 n \left(45 n^{4} + 180 n^{3} + 217 n^{2} + 84 n + 5\right)}{\left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 2\right) \left(3 n + 1\right) \left(3 n + 2\right)}\]
parts.hint_html: There are 2n constant terms in this range.

marking_points.criterion_html: Obtain \(\frac{2 n \left(45 n^{4} + 180 n^{3} + 217 n^{2} + 84 n + 5\right)}{\left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 2\right) \left(3 n + 1\right) \left(3 n + 2\right)}\).

parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: Find \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\frac{3}{\left(a r + 2\right) \left(a r + a + 2\right)}\right)\) in terms of \(a\) and \(n\).
parts.answer_html: \[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\frac{3}{\left(a r + 2\right) \left(a r + a + 2\right)}\right)=\frac{3 n}{\left(a + 2\right) \left(a n + a + 2\right)}\]
parts.solution_html:
Use the following difference, obtained by combining the terms over a common denominator:

\[\frac{3}{\left(a r + 2\right) \left(a r + a + 2\right)}=\frac{3}{a \left(a r + 2\right)}-\left(\frac{3}{a \left(a \left(r + 1\right) + 2\right)}\right)\]

Writing \(F(r)=\frac{3}{a \left(a r + 2\right)}\) and denoting the requested finite sum by \(S_n\), the cancellation is

\[\begin{aligned}S_n&=[F(1)-F(2)]\\&\quad+[F(2)-F(3)]+\cdots\\&\quad+[F(n)-F(n + 1)].\end{aligned}\]

Only the first 1 and last 1 boundary terms remain (the formula also covers overlapping boundaries).

\[S_n=\frac{3}{a \left(a + 2\right)}-\left(\frac{3}{a \left(a \left(n + 1\right) + 2\right)}\right)\]
\[S_n=\frac{3 n}{\left(a + 2\right) \left(a n + a + 2\right)}\]
parts.hint_html: Find a difference F(r)−F(r+h), then write the boundary terms before simplifying.

Obtain the correct coefficients in that representation.
Display cancellation and retain every required boundary term.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: The infinite sum is \(\frac{1}{5}\). Determine \(a\).
parts.solution_html:
Since \(a\gt 0\), the final boundary fraction tends to zero. Thus

\[\frac3{a(a+2)}=\frac15\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a^2+2a-15=0.\]
\[(a-3)(a+5)=0.\]

Reject \(a=-5\); hence \(a=3\).
parts.hint_html: Use the infinite sum before solving the quadratic.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Use the difference \((3r+1)^3-(3r-2)^3\) and the formula for \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(r\right)\) to derive the standard formula for \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(r^{2}\right)\).
parts.solution_html:
\[(3r+1)^3-(3r-2)^3=81 r^{2} - 27 r + 9\]

The successive cubic boundary terms cancel, giving

\[(3n+1)^3-1=81\sum_{r=1}^{n}r^2-27\frac{n(n+1)}2+9n.\]

Rearrange and factor:

\[81\sum_{r=1}^{n}r^2=\frac{27}{2}n(n+1)(2n+1).\]
\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(r^{2}\right)=\frac{n \left(n + 1\right) \left(2 n + 1\right)}{6}\]
parts.hint_html: The adjacent boundary values advance in steps of 3.

marking_points.criterion_html: Substitute the formula for Σr and rearrange.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html:
Define \(S_m\) by assigning weight 2 to odd-indexed squares and weight 5 to even-indexed squares:

\[S_m=2(1^2)+5(2^2)+2(3^2)+5(4^2)+\cdots+w_m m^2.\]

Find a factorised expression for \(S_{2n}\).
parts.solution_html:
Begin with weight 2 on every square, then add three more copies of each even square:

\[S_{2n}=2\sum_{r=1}^{2n}r^2+3\sum_{r=1}^{n}(2r)^2=2\sum_{r=1}^{2n}r^2+12\sum_{r=1}^{n}r^2.\]
\[S_{2n}=\frac{2 n \left(2 n + 1\right) \left(7 n + 4\right)}{3}\]

Substitute the square-sum formula at n and 2n.

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Evaluate \(\lim_{n\to\infty}S_{2n}/n^3\).
parts.solution_html: The coefficient of \(n^3\) in \(S_{2n}\) is \(\frac{28}{3}\), and all lower-degree terms vanish after division by \(n^3\).

parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html:
Use standard summation formulae to simplify

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(r \left(r + 3\right)\right)\]

in terms of \(n\).
parts.solution_html:
Expand the summand and separate its powers of \(r\).

\[r \left(r + 3\right)=r^{2} + 3 r\]

Use the standard formulae; the constant is counted once for each of the \(n\) terms.

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(r \left(r + 3\right)\right)=1\left(\frac{n \left(n + 1\right) \left(2 n + 1\right)}{6}\right)+3\left(\frac{n \left(n + 1\right)}{2}\right)\]
\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(r \left(r + 3\right)\right)=\frac{n \left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 5\right)}{3}\]
parts.hint_html: Expand before applying the standard summation formulae.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html:
Use the method of differences to find

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\frac{1}{r \left(r + 3\right)}\right)\]

in terms of \(n\).
parts.solution_html:
Use the following difference, obtained by combining the terms over a common denominator:

\[\frac{1}{r \left(r + 3\right)}=\frac{1}{3 r}-\left(\frac{1}{3 \left(r + 3\right)}\right)\]

Writing \(F(r)=\frac{1}{3 r}\) and denoting the requested finite sum by \(S_n\), the cancellation is

\[\begin{aligned}S_n&=[F(1)-F(4)]\\&\quad+[F(2)-F(5)]+\cdots\\&\quad+[F(n)-F(n + 3)].\end{aligned}\]

Only the first 3 and last 3 boundary terms remain (the formula also covers overlapping boundaries).

\[S_n=\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{9}-\left(\frac{1}{3 \left(n + 1\right)}\right)-\left(\frac{1}{3 \left(n + 2\right)}\right)-\left(\frac{1}{3 \left(n + 3\right)}\right)\]
\[S_n=\frac{n \left(11 n^{2} + 48 n + 49\right)}{18 \left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 2\right) \left(n + 3\right)}\]
parts.hint_html: Find a difference F(r)−F(r+h), then write the boundary terms before simplifying.

Obtain the correct coefficients in that representation.

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Determine whether the corresponding infinite series converges and, if it does, find its sum.
parts.solution_html:
The partial sums satisfy

\[S_n=\frac{n \left(11 n^{2} + 48 n + 49\right)}{18 \left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 2\right) \left(n + 3\right)}\]

Taking the limit as \(n\to\infty\) gives a finite number:

\[\lim_{n\to\infty}S_n=\frac{11}{18}\]

Therefore the series converges to this value.
parts.hint_html: Use the finite partial sum, not a sum of separate divergent series.
parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html:
Use standard summation formulae to simplify

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(- r^{2} - 5 r - 2\right)\]

in terms of \(n\).
parts.solution_html:
Expand the summand and separate its powers of \(r\).

\[- r^{2} - 5 r - 2=- r^{2} - 5 r - 2\]

Use the standard formulae; the constant is counted once for each of the \(n\) terms.

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(- r^{2} - 5 r - 2\right)=-1\left(\frac{n \left(n + 1\right) \left(2 n + 1\right)}{6}\right)-5\left(\frac{n \left(n + 1\right)}{2}\right)-2\left(n\right)\]
\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(- r^{2} - 5 r - 2\right)=- \frac{n \left(n + 2\right) \left(n + 7\right)}{3}\]
parts.hint_html: Expand before applying the standard summation formulae.

marking_points.criterion_html: Expand and separate the polynomial into standard sums.
Apply the summation formulae with the correct limits and number of constant terms.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html:
Show that

\[- \frac{r^{2} + 5 r + 2}{\left(r^{2} + 4 r + 8\right) \left(r^{2} + 6 r + 13\right)}=\frac{r + 3}{\left(r + 3\right)^{2} + 4}-\frac{r + 2}{\left(r + 2\right)^{2} + 4}\]
parts.solution_html:
The numerator after taking a common denominator is

\[(r+3)\big((r+2)^2+4\big)-(r+2)\big((r+3)^2+4\big)\]
\[4-(r+2)(r+3)=- r^{2} - 5 r - 2\]

This is the numerator on the left.
parts.hint_html: Keep the factors before expanding; the cubic terms cancel.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Hence find \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(- \frac{r^{2} + 5 r + 2}{\left(r^{2} + 4 r + 8\right) \left(r^{2} + 6 r + 13\right)}\right)\) and its limit as \(n\to\infty\).
parts.solution_html:
Writing \(F(r)=\frac{r + 2}{\left(r + 2\right)^{2} + 4}\), the sum is

\[[F(2)-F(1)]+[F(3)-F(2)]+\cdots+[F(n+1)-F(n)]=F(n+1)-F(1).\]
\[S_n=- \frac{n \left(3 n + 5\right)}{13 \left(n^{2} + 6 n + 13\right)}\]

The rational boundary value \(F(n+1)\) tends to 0, not to a nonzero constant. Thus the limit is \(- \frac{3}{13}\).
parts.hint_html: The order here is F(r+1)−F(r), so preserve the sign.

marking_points.criterion_html: Take the limit of the boundary term.

parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html:
Use standard summation formulae to simplify

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(r \left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 4\right)\right)\]

in terms of \(n\).
parts.solution_html:
Expand the summand and separate its powers of \(r\).

\[r \left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 4\right)=r^{3} + 6 r^{2} + 8 r\]

Use the standard formulae; the constant is counted once for each of the \(n\) terms.

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(r \left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 4\right)\right)=1\left(\frac{n^{2} \left(n + 1\right)^{2}}{4}\right)+6\left(\frac{n \left(n + 1\right) \left(2 n + 1\right)}{6}\right)+8\left(\frac{n \left(n + 1\right)}{2}\right)\]
\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(r \left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 4\right)\right)=\frac{n \left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 4\right) \left(n + 5\right)}{4}\]
parts.hint_html: Expand before applying the standard summation formulae.

marking_points.criterion_html: Expand and separate the polynomial into standard sums.
Apply the summation formulae with the correct limits and number of constant terms.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html:
Use the method of differences to find

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\frac{1}{r \left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 4\right)}\right)\]

in terms of \(n\).
parts.solution_html:
Use the following difference, obtained by combining the terms over a common denominator:

\[\frac{1}{r \left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 4\right)}=\frac{1}{4 r \left(r + 2\right)}-\left(\frac{1}{4 \left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 4\right)}\right)\]

Writing \(F(r)=\frac{1}{4 r \left(r + 2\right)}\) and denoting the requested finite sum by \(S_n\), the cancellation is

\[\begin{aligned}S_n&=[F(1)-F(3)]\\&\quad+[F(2)-F(4)]+\cdots\\&\quad+[F(n)-F(n + 2)].\end{aligned}\]

Only the first 2 and last 2 boundary terms remain (the formula also covers overlapping boundaries).

\[S_n=\frac{1}{12}+\frac{1}{32}-\left(\frac{1}{4 \left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 3\right)}\right)-\left(\frac{1}{4 \left(n + 2\right) \left(n + 4\right)}\right)\]
\[S_n=\frac{n \left(n + 5\right) \left(11 n^{2} + 55 n + 62\right)}{96 \left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 2\right) \left(n + 3\right) \left(n + 4\right)}\]
parts.hint_html: Find a difference F(r)−F(r+h), then write the boundary terms before simplifying.

marking_points.criterion_html: Find an appropriate partial-fraction or difference representation.
Obtain the correct coefficients in that representation.
Display cancellation and retain every required boundary term.

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Determine whether the corresponding infinite series converges and, if it does, find its sum.
parts.solution_html:
The partial sums satisfy

\[S_n=\frac{n \left(n + 5\right) \left(11 n^{2} + 55 n + 62\right)}{96 \left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 2\right) \left(n + 3\right) \left(n + 4\right)}\]

Taking the limit as \(n\to\infty\) gives a finite number:

\[\lim_{n\to\infty}S_n=\frac{11}{96}\]

Therefore the series converges to this value.
parts.hint_html: Use the finite partial sum, not a sum of separate divergent series.

marking_points.criterion_html: Take the limit of the partial sum and justify the limiting boundary value(s).

parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: Find \(\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2\).
parts.solution_html: Vieta gives \(\alpha+\beta+\gamma=-3\) and \(\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha=2\). Hence the square sum is \(9-4=5\).
parts.hint_html: Use the first two coefficient relations.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find \(\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3\).
parts.solution_html:
Sum the cubic equation over its three roots:

\[P_3+3P_2+2P_1-12=0.\]
\[P_3=-15+6+12=3.\]
parts.hint_html: The constant −4 appears three times.

marking_points.criterion_html: Sum the original cubic over the roots.

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html:
Find a factorised expression for

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left[(2r+\alpha)^3+(2r+\beta)^3+(2r+\gamma)^3\right].\]
parts.solution_html:
At a fixed index, the bracket is

\[24r^3+12r^2P_1+6rP_2+P_3=24 r^{3} - 36 r^{2} + 30 r + 3\]

Expand the summand and separate its powers of \(r\).

\[24 r^{3} - 36 r^{2} + 30 r + 3=24 r^{3} - 36 r^{2} + 30 r + 3\]

Use the standard formulae; the constant is counted once for each of the \(n\) terms.

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(24 r^{3} - 36 r^{2} + 30 r + 3\right)=24\left(\frac{n^{2} \left(n + 1\right)^{2}}{4}\right)-36\left(\frac{n \left(n + 1\right) \left(2 n + 1\right)}{6}\right)+30\left(\frac{n \left(n + 1\right)}{2}\right)+3\left(n\right)\]
\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(24 r^{3} - 36 r^{2} + 30 r + 3\right)=3 n \left(2 n^{3} + n + 4\right)\]
parts.hint_html: Expand one shifted cube, then combine the root sums.

marking_points.criterion_html: Collect the coefficients of r³, r² and r.
Apply the standard sums of cubes, squares and integers.
Collect all terms, including the constant contribution.

parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html:
Use standard summation formulae to simplify

\[\sum_{r=2}^{n + 1}\left(\left(5 r + 2\right) \left(5 r + 7\right)\right)\]

in terms of \(n\).
parts.solution_html:
Let \(F(m)=\sum_{r=1}^{m}(\left(5 r + 2\right) \left(5 r + 7\right))\). Use the standard formulae to obtain the partial-sum polynomial, then subtract the value one index before the lower limit.

\[F(m)=\frac{m \left(25 m^{2} + 105 m + 122\right)}{3}\]
\[\sum_{r=2}^{n + 1}\left(\left(5 r + 2\right) \left(5 r + 7\right)\right)=F(n + 1)-F(1)\]
\[\sum_{r=2}^{n + 1}\left(\left(5 r + 2\right) \left(5 r + 7\right)\right)=\frac{n \left(25 n^{2} + 180 n + 407\right)}{3}\]
parts.hint_html: Expand before applying the standard summation formulae.

marking_points.criterion_html: Expand and separate the polynomial into standard sums.
Apply the summation formulae with the correct limits and number of constant terms.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html:
Use the method of differences to find

\[\sum_{r=2}^{n + 1}\left(\frac{1}{\left(5 r + 2\right) \left(5 r + 7\right)}\right)\]

in terms of \(n\).
parts.solution_html:
Use the following difference, obtained by combining the terms over a common denominator:

\[\frac{1}{\left(5 r + 2\right) \left(5 r + 7\right)}=\frac{1}{25 r + 10}-\left(\frac{1}{25 r + 35}\right)\]

Writing \(F(r)=\frac{1}{25 r + 10}\) and denoting the requested finite sum by \(S_n\), the cancellation is

\[\begin{aligned}S_n&=[F(2)-F(3)]\\&\quad+[F(3)-F(4)]+\cdots\\&\quad+[F(n + 1)-F(n + 2)].\end{aligned}\]

Only the first 1 and last 1 boundary terms remain (the formula also covers overlapping boundaries).

\[S_n=\frac{1}{60}-\left(\frac{1}{25 n + 60}\right)\]
\[S_n=\frac{n}{12 \left(5 n + 12\right)}\]
parts.hint_html: Find a difference F(r)−F(r+h), then write the boundary terms before simplifying.

Obtain the correct coefficients in that representation.
Display cancellation and retain every required boundary term.

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Determine whether the corresponding infinite series converges and, if it does, find its sum.
parts.solution_html:
The partial sums satisfy

\[S_n=\frac{n}{12 \left(5 n + 12\right)}\]

Taking the limit as \(n\to\infty\) gives a finite number:

\[\lim_{n\to\infty}S_n=\frac{1}{60}\]

Therefore the series converges to this value.
parts.hint_html: Use the finite partial sum, not a sum of separate divergent series.
parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: For \(n\ge3\), use partial fractions and the method of differences to find \(\sum_{r=3}^{n}\left(\frac{1}{r^{2} - 4}\right)\).
parts.solution_html:
Use the following difference, obtained by combining the terms over a common denominator:

\[\frac{1}{r^{2} - 4}=\frac{1}{4 r - 8}-\left(\frac{1}{4 r + 8}\right)\]

Writing \(F(r)=\frac{1}{4 r - 8}\) and denoting the requested finite sum by \(S_n\), the cancellation is

\[\begin{aligned}S_n&=[F(3)-F(7)]\\&\quad+[F(4)-F(8)]+\cdots\\&\quad+[F(n)-F(n + 4)].\end{aligned}\]

Only the first 4 and last 4 boundary terms remain (the formula also covers overlapping boundaries).

\[S_n=\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{8}+\frac{1}{12}+\frac{1}{16}-\left(\frac{1}{4 n - 4}\right)-\left(\frac{1}{4 n}\right)-\left(\frac{1}{4 n + 4}\right)-\left(\frac{1}{4 n + 8}\right)\]
\[S_n=\frac{\left(n - 2\right) \left(25 n^{3} + 52 n^{2} + 7 n - 12\right)}{48 n \left(n - 1\right) \left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 2\right)}\]
parts.hint_html: Find a difference F(r)−F(r+h), then write the boundary terms before simplifying.

marking_points.criterion_html: Find an appropriate partial-fraction or difference representation.
Obtain the correct coefficients in that representation.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Determine whether the corresponding infinite series converges and, if it does, find its sum.
parts.solution_html:
The partial sums satisfy

\[S_n=\frac{\left(n - 2\right) \left(25 n^{3} + 52 n^{2} + 7 n - 12\right)}{48 n \left(n - 1\right) \left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 2\right)}\]

Taking the limit as \(n\to\infty\) gives a finite number:

\[\lim_{n\to\infty}S_n=\frac{25}{48}\]

Therefore the series converges to this value.
parts.hint_html: Use the finite partial sum, not a sum of separate divergent series.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html:
Evaluate

\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{r=n + 1}^{3 n}\left(\frac{n}{r^{2} - 4}\right).\]
parts.solution_html:
First keep the window finite:

\[T_n=n\big(S_{3n}-S_n\big)\]
\[T_n=\frac n4\left[\frac1{n-1}+\frac1n+\frac1{n+1}+\frac1{n+2}-\frac1{3n-1}-\frac1{3n}-\frac1{3n+1}-\frac1{3n+2}\right].\]

The four positive scaled fractions tend to 1; the four subtracted scaled fractions tend to \(\frac{1}{3}\). Hence

\[\lim T_n=\frac14\left(4-\frac43\right)=\frac23.\]
parts.hint_html: Find the exact moving sum before taking the limit.

marking_points.criterion_html: Retain all four boundary terms from each partial sum.

parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html:
Use the method of differences to find

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\frac{1}{\left(4 r - 1\right) \left(4 r + 3\right)}\right)\]

in terms of \(n\).
parts.solution_html:
Use the following difference, obtained by combining the terms over a common denominator:

\[\frac{1}{\left(4 r - 1\right) \left(4 r + 3\right)}=\frac{1}{16 r - 4}-\left(\frac{1}{16 r + 12}\right)\]

Writing \(F(r)=\frac{1}{16 r - 4}\) and denoting the requested finite sum by \(S_n\), the cancellation is

\[\begin{aligned}S_n&=[F(1)-F(2)]\\&\quad+[F(2)-F(3)]+\cdots\\&\quad+[F(n)-F(n + 1)].\end{aligned}\]

Only the first 1 and last 1 boundary terms remain (the formula also covers overlapping boundaries).

\[S_n=\frac{1}{12}-\left(\frac{1}{16 n + 12}\right)\]
\[S_n=\frac{n}{3 \left(4 n + 3\right)}\]
parts.hint_html: Find a difference F(r)−F(r+h), then write the boundary terms before simplifying.

marking_points.criterion_html: Find an appropriate partial-fraction or difference representation.
Obtain the correct coefficients in that representation.
Display cancellation and retain every required boundary term.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html:
Evaluate

\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{r=n + 1}^{n^{2} + n}\left(\frac{n}{\left(4 r - 1\right) \left(4 r + 3\right)}\right).\]
parts.solution_html:
The finite window is

\[T_n=\frac{n^{3}}{\left(4 n + 3\right) \left(4 n^{2} + 4 n + 3\right)}\]

Equivalently,

\[T_n=\frac{n}{4(4n+3)}-\frac{n}{4(4n^2+4n+3)}.\]

The first term tends to \(\frac{1}{16}\); the second tends to zero.
parts.hint_html: The upper endpoint grows quadratically, while the lower endpoint grows linearly.

marking_points.criterion_html: Use a difference of the two partial sums.
Use the endpoints n+1 and n²+n+1 correctly.

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html:
Use standard summation formulae to simplify

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\left(4 r + 1\right) \left(4 r + 5\right)\right)\]

in terms of \(n\).
parts.solution_html:
Expand the summand and separate its powers of \(r\).

\[\left(4 r + 1\right) \left(4 r + 5\right)=16 r^{2} + 24 r + 5\]

Use the standard formulae; the constant is counted once for each of the \(n\) terms.

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\left(4 r + 1\right) \left(4 r + 5\right)\right)=16\left(\frac{n \left(n + 1\right) \left(2 n + 1\right)}{6}\right)+24\left(\frac{n \left(n + 1\right)}{2}\right)+5\left(n\right)\]
\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\left(4 r + 1\right) \left(4 r + 5\right)\right)=\frac{n \left(16 n^{2} + 60 n + 59\right)}{3}\]
parts.hint_html: Expand before applying the standard summation formulae.

Apply the summation formulae with the correct limits and number of constant terms.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html:
Use the method of differences to find

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\frac{1}{\left(4 r + 1\right) \left(4 r + 5\right)}\right)\]

in terms of \(n\).
parts.solution_html:
Use the following difference, obtained by combining the terms over a common denominator:

\[\frac{1}{\left(4 r + 1\right) \left(4 r + 5\right)}=\frac{1}{16 r + 4}-\left(\frac{1}{16 r + 20}\right)\]

Writing \(F(r)=\frac{1}{16 r + 4}\) and denoting the requested finite sum by \(S_n\), the cancellation is

\[\begin{aligned}S_n&=[F(1)-F(2)]\\&\quad+[F(2)-F(3)]+\cdots\\&\quad+[F(n)-F(n + 1)].\end{aligned}\]

Only the first 1 and last 1 boundary terms remain (the formula also covers overlapping boundaries).

\[S_n=\frac{1}{20}-\left(\frac{1}{16 n + 20}\right)\]
\[S_n=\frac{n}{5 \left(4 n + 5\right)}\]

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Let \(P_n\) be the polynomial sum in part (a) and \(T_n\) the reciprocal sum in part (b). Find \(\lim_{n\to\infty}n^{-3}P_nT_n\).
parts.solution_html:
The two factors have limits

\[\frac{P_n}{n^3}\to\frac{16}{3},\qquad T_n\to\frac1{20}.\]
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{P_nT_n}{n^3}=\frac{16}{3}\cdot\frac1{20}=\frac4{15}.\]
parts.hint_html: Take the limit of P_n/n³ and T_n separately.
parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: Find a simplified expression for \(S_{2n}\).
parts.solution_html:
Pair successive terms:

\[(6r-4)^2-(6r-1)^2=15-36r.\]
\[S_{2n}=15n-36\frac{n(n+1)}2=-3n(6n+1).\]

Alternatively, subtract twice the even-indexed terms from the full quadratic sum.
parts.hint_html: Pair the terms or subtract twice the even-indexed square sum.
parts.label: a

parts.solution_html:
The next term is positive and equals \((6n+2)^2\). Thus

\[S_{2n+1}=S_{2n}+(6n+2)^2=18 n^{2} + 21 n + 4\]
parts.hint_html: Append exactly the next positive term.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find the limits of \(S_{2n}/n^2\) and \(S_{2n+1}/n^2\).
parts.solution_html: After division by \(n^2\), the lower-degree terms vanish. The leading coefficients are −18 and 18 respectively.
parts.hint_html: Do not assume the two parity subsequences have the same limit.
parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: Find \(S_n=\sum_{r=1}^{n}u_r\) in terms of \(t\) and \(n\).
parts.solution_html:
Separate the two geometric differences. In each, only the first term and final subtracted term survive:

\[S_n=2t-(2t)^{n+1}+5t-(5t)^{n+1}.\]
\[S_n=7 t - \left(2 t\right)^{n + 1} - \left(5 t\right)^{n + 1}\]
parts.hint_html: Treat the two geometric differences separately.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Determine every real value of \(t\) for which the infinite series converges, and give its sum in each case.
parts.answer_html:
\[-\frac15\lt t\le\frac15.\]

For \(-\frac15\lt t\lt \frac15\), the sum is \(7t\). At \(t=1/5\), it is \(2/5\).
parts.solution_html:
When \(|5t|\lt 1\), both final powers tend to zero, so the sum is \(7t\). At \(t=1/5\), the term \((5t)^{n+1}\) is identically 1 while \((2t)^{n+1}\to0\), giving \(7/5-1=2/5\).

At \(t=-1/5\), the surviving \((-1)^{n+1}\) term oscillates, so no limit exists. If \(|t|\gt 1/5\), factor the two powers as

\[(5t)^{n+1}\left[1+(2/5)^{n+1}\right].\]

Its magnitude grows without bound; the smaller power cannot cancel the dominant one. These cases exhaust the real line.
parts.hint_html: Check t=1/5 and t=−1/5 directly instead of applying only |5t|<1.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find all values of \(t\) for which the sum to infinity equals \(2/5\).
parts.solution_html: In the open interval solve \(7t=2/5\), giving \(t=2/35\). This lies in the required interval. The separately evaluated endpoint \(t=1/5\) also gives the prescribed sum.
parts.hint_html: Use the piecewise answer from part (b).
parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: Set \(t=1/10\). Find the least integer \(n\) for which \(S_\infty-S_n\lt 10^{-4}\).
parts.solution_html:
The exact positive remainder is

\[R_n=(1/5)^{n+1}+(1/2)^{n+1}.\]

It is strictly decreasing. At \(n=12\), \(R_{12}\gt 2^{-13}\gt 10^{-4}\). At \(n=13\), \(R_{13}=5^{-14}+2^{-14}\lt 10^{-4}\). Therefore 13 is the least value.
parts.hint_html: Check the two integers around the threshold and use monotonicity.

marking_points.criterion_html: Check that n=12 fails and n=13 succeeds.

parts.label: d

parts.prompt_html: Verify that \(u_r=F(r)-F(r+1)\), where \(F(r)=e^{-2r}/(r+1)\).
parts.solution_html: Take the common denominator \((r+1)(r+2)e^{2r+2}\). The numerator is \((r+2)e^2-(r+1)\), as required.
parts.hint_html: Multiply the first numerator by e² when matching denominators.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find \(S_n=\sum_{r=1}^{n}u_r\) and its sum to infinity \(S\).
parts.solution_html: The boundary terms are \(F(1)-F(n+1)\). The final term tends to zero, giving the stated limit.
parts.hint_html: The last denominator is n+2.

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find the least \(n\) such that \((n+2)(S-S_n)\lt 10^{-7}\).
parts.solution_html:
\[e^{-2n-2}\lt 10^{-7}\iff 2n+2\gt 7\ln10\iff n\gt \frac72\ln10-1\approx7.059.\]

Hence the least integer is 8.
parts.hint_html: Take natural logarithms; remember the inequality is strict.

Use standard summation formulae to simplify

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\left(6 r + 1\right) \left(6 r + 7\right)\right)\]

in terms of \(n\).

Expand the summand and separate its powers of \(r\).

\[\left(6 r + 1\right) \left(6 r + 7\right)=36 r^{2} + 48 r + 7\]

Use the standard formulae; the constant is counted once for each of the \(n\) terms.

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\left(6 r + 1\right) \left(6 r + 7\right)\right)=36\left(\frac{n \left(n + 1\right) \left(2 n + 1\right)}{6}\right)+48\left(\frac{n \left(n + 1\right)}{2}\right)+7\left(n\right)\]

parts.prompt_html:

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\frac{1}{\left(6 r + 1\right) \left(6 r + 7\right)}\right)\]

in terms of \(n\).
parts.solution_html:
Use the following difference, obtained by combining the terms over a common denominator:

\[\frac{1}{\left(6 r + 1\right) \left(6 r + 7\right)}=\frac{1}{36 r + 6}-\left(\frac{1}{36 r + 42}\right)\]

parts.prompt_html: Let \(P_n\) and \(T_n\) denote the sums in (a) and (b). Prove that \(P_n/T_n\) is an integer for every positive integer \(n\).

Simplifying the reciprocal sum gives \(T_n=n/[7(6n+7)]\). Therefore

parts.prompt_html: Find \(u_r\) and justify that your expression is valid also when \(r=1\).

\[T_n=S_{3n}-S_n\]

\[S_n=\frac{(3n+2)(3n+5)}{(n+1)(n+2)}-5.\]

parts.prompt_html: Use this identity and the formula for \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(r\right)\) to derive the standard formula for \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(r^{3}\right)\).
parts.solution_html:
The two-step difference leaves two upper and two lower boundary terms:

\[n^4+(n+1)^4-0^4-1^4=8\sum_{r=1}^{n}r^3+8\frac{n(n+1)}2.\]

Subtract \(4n(n+1)\) and simplify to obtain

\[8\sum r^3=2n^2(n+1)^2.\]

parts.prompt_html:
Prove by mathematical induction that

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\frac{2 r + 5}{\left(r + 1\right) \left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 3\right) \left(r + 4\right)}\right)=\frac{1}{8} - \frac{1}{\left(n + 2\right) \left(n + 4\right)}\]

for every positive integer \(n\).
parts.answer_html: The identity holds for all positive integers \(n\).
parts.solution_html:
Base case. For \(n=1\), the left side is \(\frac{7}{120}\); the right side is \(1/8-1/15=7/120\).

Inductive hypothesis. Assume the formula is true at \(n=k\), for an arbitrary positive integer \(k\).

\[S_{k+1}=\frac18-\frac1{(k+2)(k+4)}+\frac{2k+7}{(k+2)(k+3)(k+4)(k+5)}.\]

The last two terms combine to

\[\frac{-(k+3)(k+5)+(2k+7)}{(k+2)(k+3)(k+4)(k+5)}=\frac{-(k+2)(k+4)}{(k+2)(k+3)(k+4)(k+5)}=-\frac1{(k+3)(k+5)}.\]

Thus \(S_{k+1}=1/8-1/[(k+3)(k+5)]\), exactly the required formula at \(k+1\). The base case and implication prove the result for every positive integer.
parts.hint_html: After adding u_(k+1), combine only the two remainder fractions.

parts.prompt_html:
Verify that

\[(2r)^4-(2r-2)^4=8(2r-1)^3+8(2r-1).\]
parts.hint_html: Use the midpoint 2r−1.

marking_points.criterion_html: Verify the identity by expansion or midpoint substitution.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Using this identity and \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}(2r-1)=n^2\), derive a formula for \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\left(2 r - 1\right)^{3}\right)\).
parts.solution_html:
The left side telescopes from \(0^4\) to \((2n)^4\). Hence

\[16n^4=8\sum_{r=1}^{n}(2r-1)^3+8n^2.\]

Rearranging gives

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\left(2 r - 1\right)^{3}\right)=n^{2} \left(2 n^{2} - 1\right)\]
parts.hint_html: The identity follows the even boundary sequence 0,2,4,…,2n.

marking_points.criterion_html: Substitute the sum of odd integers as n².

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html:
Use standard summation formulae to simplify

\[\sum_{r=2 n}^{5 n}\left(r^{2}\right)\]

in terms of \(n\).
parts.solution_html:
Let \(F(m)=\sum_{r=1}^{m}(r^{2})\). Use the standard formulae to obtain the partial-sum polynomial, then subtract the value one index before the lower limit.

\[F(m)=\frac{m \left(m + 1\right) \left(2 m + 1\right)}{6}\]
\[\sum_{r=2 n}^{5 n}\left(r^{2}\right)=F(5 n)-F(2 n - 1)\]
\[\sum_{r=2 n}^{5 n}\left(r^{2}\right)=\frac{n \left(3 n + 1\right) \left(26 n + 1\right)}{2}\]
parts.hint_html: Expand before applying the standard summation formulae.

marking_points.criterion_html: Expand and separate the polynomial into standard sums.
Apply the summation formulae with the correct limits and number of constant terms.
Substitute and collect the polynomial coefficients correctly.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Use the given identity to find a simplified expression for \(T_n\).
parts.solution_html:
Set \(z=2r-1\) in the identity, then sum. The even sixth-power boundaries cancel:

\[(2n)^6=12T_n+40\sum_{r=1}^{n}(2r-1)^3+12\sum_{r=1}^{n}(2r-1).\]

Use the two supplied lower-power results:

\[64n^6=12T_n+40n^2(2n^2-1)+12n^2.\]
\[12T_n=64n^6-80n^4+28n^2.\]
\[T_n=\frac{n^{2} \left(16 n^{4} - 20 n^{2} + 7\right)}{3}\]
parts.hint_html: Substitute the odd value 2r−1 before summing the identity.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Evaluate \(\lim_{n\to\infty}n^{-\lambda}T_n\) when (i) \(\lambda=6\) and (ii) \(\lambda\gt 6\).
parts.solution_html: The leading term is \(16n^6/3\). At \(\lambda=6\) the remaining powers vanish; at \(\lambda\gt 6\) every exponent after division is negative.
parts.hint_html: Compare λ with the degree of the partial-sum polynomial.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(9 r^{2}\right)\).
parts.solution_html: \[A_n=9\sum_{r=1}^{n}r^2=\frac32n(n+1)(2n+1).\]
parts.hint_html: Take the factor 9 outside the sum.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: A sum includes the squares of all integers from 1 to \(3n\), but each square whose index is a multiple of 3 is subtracted rather than added. Find this sum.
parts.solution_html:
Start with every square positive. To reverse the sign of a selected square, subtract it twice:

\[B_n=\sum_{r=1}^{3n}r^2-2\sum_{r=1}^{n}(3r)^2.\]
\[B_n=\frac{n \left(6 n^{2} - 9 n - 5\right)}{2}\]
parts.hint_html: Changing a sign requires subtracting twice, not once.

marking_points.criterion_html: Use the full square sum up to 3n.

parts.label: b

parts.solution_html:
The common numerator is

\[(r+2)^3-(r+1)^3=3r^2+9r+7.\]
parts.hint_html: Expand the difference of the two cubes.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find \(S_n=\sum_{r=1}^{n}u_r\) and the infinite sum \(S\).
parts.solution_html: Only \(1/2^3\) and \(-1/(n+2)^3\) remain after cancellation. The latter tends to zero.
parts.hint_html: The first positive denominator is 2³.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find the least \(n\) such that \(S-S_n\lt 10^{-12}\).
parts.solution_html:
\[\frac1{(n+2)^3}\lt 10^{-12}\iff n+2\gt 10^4\iff n\gt 9998.\]

At \(n=9998\) equality holds, so that integer is not allowed. The least value is 9999.
parts.hint_html: Distinguish strict inequality from equality at the boundary.
parts.label: c

parts.solution_html:
Factor out the five common factors:

\[w_{r+1}-w_r=(r+1)(r+2)(r+3)(r+4)(r+5)\big[(r+6)-r\big].\]

The bracket is 6.
parts.hint_html: Do not expand the six-factor product.
parts.label: a

parts.solution_html:
From (a), \(6u_r=w_{r+1}-w_r\). Therefore

\[6\sum_{r=1}^{n}u_r=w_{n+1}-w_1.\]

Use \(w_1=6!=720\) to obtain the stated formula.
parts.hint_html: The first boundary product is 6!, not 5!.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: For a real number \(x\), define \(v_r=x^{w_r}-x^{w_{r+1}}\). Determine all \(x\) for which \(\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}v_r\) converges, and give its sum.
parts.answer_html:
\[-1\le x\le1.\]

The sum is \(x^{720}\) for \(-1\lt x\lt 1\), and 0 at \(x=-1\) or \(x=1\).
parts.solution_html: The finite sum is \(x^{720}-x^{w_{n+1}}\). The exponents are positive even integers tending to infinity. For \(|x|\lt 1\), the final power tends to zero; this includes \(x=0\). At \(x=1\) and \(x=-1\), every power is 1, so every term is zero. For \(|x|\gt 1\), the even powers grow without bound, so the partial sums have no finite limit.
parts.hint_html: All six-factor products are even. Check x=±1 directly.

marking_points.criterion_html: Obtain the telescoping partial sum and use the growing exponents.
Include both endpoints with sum zero and exclude |x|>1.

parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: Express \(S_n=\sum_{r=1}^{n}u_r\) in terms of \(x\), \(n\) and \(f\).
parts.solution_html:
All intermediate powers cancel:

\[[x^{f(2)}-x^{f(1)}]+[x^{f(3)}-x^{f(2)}]+\cdots+[x^{f(n+1)}-x^{f(n)}].\]
parts.hint_html: Keep the order of the difference as written.

marking_points.criterion_html: Obtain the two correctly signed boundary powers.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Take \(f(r)=\ln(r+1)\). Determine the set of \(x\) for which the infinite series converges, and its sum in each case.
parts.answer_html:
\[0\lt x\le1.\]

For \(0\lt x\lt 1\), the sum is \(-2^{\ln x}\). At \(x=1\) it is 0.
parts.solution_html:
Use \(x^{\ln(r+1)}=(r+1)^{\ln x}\) to get

\[S_n=(n+2)^{\ln x}-2^{\ln x}.\]

For \(0\lt x\lt 1\), the exponent \(\ln x\) is negative, so the first term tends to zero. At \(x=1\) it is constantly 1 and the difference is zero. For \(x\gt 1\) it grows without bound.
parts.hint_html: The sign of ln x controls the power of n+2.

marking_points.criterion_html: Give the correct open-interval convergence and sum.

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Instead take \(f(r)=3\log_x(r+1)\), with \(x\ne1\). Find and factorise \(\sum_{n=1}^{N}S_n\).
parts.solution_html:
Because \(x\gt 0\) and \(x\ne1\),

\[x^{3\log_x(r+1)}=(r+1)^3,\qquad S_n=(n+2)^3-8=n^3+6n^2+12n.\]
\[\sum_{n=1}^{N}S_n=\frac{N^2(N+1)^2}{4}+N(N+1)(2N+1)+6N(N+1).\]
\[\sum_{n=1}^{N}S_n=\frac{N \left(N + 1\right) \left(N^{2} + 9 N + 28\right)}{4}\]
parts.hint_html: First simplify S_n, then apply the standard formulae to the second sum.
parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: Find \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(u_r\right)\) in terms of \(n\) and \(x\).
parts.solution_html:
Write \(q=e^{2x}\), so \(q\gt 0\) and \(q\ne1\). Then

\[u_r=q^r(q-1)^2=(q-1)(q^{r+1}-q^r).\]

The geometric differences cancel:

\[S_n=(q-1)(q^{n+1}-q)=q(q-1)(q^n-1).\]

Replace \(q\) by \(e^{2x}\).
parts.hint_html: Factor out q−1 after setting q=e^(2x).

marking_points.criterion_html: Use q=e^(2x) or an equivalent geometric representation.
Express the summand as a constant times a difference.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: For nonzero real \(x\), determine when the infinite series converges and find its sum.
parts.solution_html: If \(x\lt 0\), then \(0\lt q\lt 1\) and \(q^n\to0\), so \(S=q(1-q)\). If \(x\gt 0\), then \(q\gt 1\) and the positive partial sums diverge to infinity.
parts.hint_html: The variable x is an exponent, so x<0 corresponds to a ratio below 1.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}\ln u_r\).
parts.solution_html:
For every allowed \(x\), \(u_r\gt 0\). The square must be handled with an absolute value:

\[\ln u_r=2rx+2\ln|e^{2x}-1|.\]

Summing gives \(2x\cdot n(n+1)/2\) plus \(n\) copies of the logarithmic constant.
parts.hint_html: Use ln(z²)=2 ln|z|; z may be negative.

marking_points.criterion_html: Use the absolute value in the constant logarithm.

parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: Show that \(u_r=\tan(A_r+\pi/3)-\tan A_r\).
parts.solution_html:
\[\tan B-\tan A=\frac{\sin B\cos A-\cos B\sin A}{\cos A\cos B}=\frac{\sin(B-A)}{\cos A\cos B}.\]

Use \(B=A_r+\pi/3\). The denominators are nonzero: their angles have numerators \(4r+1\) or \(4r+5\) in units of \(\pi/12\), never \(6+12m\).
parts.hint_html: Use the sine difference formula in the numerator.

marking_points.criterion_html: Put the tangent difference over a common denominator.

parts.label: a

parts.solution_html: Since \(A_{r+1}=A_r+\pi/3\), the sum is \(\tan A_n-\tan A_0\).
parts.hint_html: There are n terms, from r=0 to r=n−1.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Prove that the infinite series does not converge.
parts.solution_html:
\[S_{3m}=0,\qquad S_{3m+1}=\tan\frac{5\pi}{12}-\tan\frac\pi{12}=2\sqrt3.\]

The two infinite subsequences have different constant values, so the partial sums cannot have a common limit.
parts.hint_html: Examine indices congruent to 0 and 1 modulo 3.
parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: Find \(S_n\) and its limit \(S\).
parts.solution_html:
Split each logarithm as

\[\ln\frac{(r+1)(r+3)}{(r+2)^2}=\ln\frac{r+1}{r+2}-\ln\frac{r+2}{r+3}.\]

The difference telescopes to

\[S_n=\ln\frac23-\ln\frac{n+2}{n+3}=\ln\frac{2(n+3)}{3(n+2)}.\]

All logarithm arguments are positive. Taking the limit yields \(\ln(2/3)\).
parts.hint_html: Use a difference of logarithms of consecutive ratios.

marking_points.criterion_html: Split the logarithm into a telescoping difference.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find the least \(n\) such that \(S_n-S\lt 0.002\).
parts.solution_html:
\[S_n-S=\ln\left(1+\frac1{n+2}\right).\]

Because the exponential function is increasing,

\[\ln\left(1+\frac1{n+2}\right)\lt 0.002\iff n\gt \frac1{e^{0.002}-1}-2\approx497.5002.\]

Thus \(n=498\). At \(n=497\) the error is \(\ln(500/499)\gt 0.002\); at \(n=498\) it is \(\ln(501/500)\lt 0.002\).
parts.hint_html: Exponentiate the inequality rather than replacing ln(1+z) by z.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html:
Use a sum-to-product identity to show that

\[u_r=\sec\left(\frac{r\pi}{3}+\frac{5\pi}{12}\right)-\sec\left(\frac{r\pi}{3}+\frac\pi{12}\right).\]
parts.solution_html:
Write \(A=r\pi/3+\pi/12\) and \(B=A+\pi/3\). Then

\[\cos A-\cos B=2\sin\frac{A+B}{2}\sin\frac{B-A}{2}=\sin\left(\frac{r\pi}{3}+\frac\pi4\right).\]

Divide by \(\cos A\cos B\). Neither denominator vanishes for integral \(r\).
parts.hint_html: Write sec B−sec A as (cos A−cos B)/(cos A cos B).
parts.label: a

parts.solution_html: The two arguments in each difference are successive members of the same angle sequence. All intermediate secants cancel.
parts.hint_html: Use the initial angle π/12 and the angle after N increments.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Explain why the corresponding infinite series does not converge.
parts.solution_html:
\[S_{6m}=0,\qquad S_{6m+3}=-2\sec\frac\pi{12}.\]

These distinct subsequential values rule out a limit.
parts.hint_html: Compare N=6m and N=6m+3.

marking_points.criterion_html: Give a valid nonconvergence argument using distinct subsequences.

parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html:
Use standard summation formulae to simplify

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(64 r^{3} + 16 r\right)\]

in terms of \(n\).
parts.solution_html:
Expand the summand and separate its powers of \(r\).

\[64 r^{3} + 16 r=64 r^{3} + 16 r\]

Use the standard formulae; the constant is counted once for each of the \(n\) terms.

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(64 r^{3} + 16 r\right)=64\left(\frac{n^{2} \left(n + 1\right)^{2}}{4}\right)+16\left(\frac{n \left(n + 1\right)}{2}\right)\]
\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(64 r^{3} + 16 r\right)=8 n \left(n + 1\right) \left(2 n^{2} + 2 n + 1\right)\]
parts.hint_html: Expand before applying the standard summation formulae.

marking_points.criterion_html: Expand and separate the polynomial into standard sums.
Apply the summation formulae with the correct limits and number of constant terms.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html:
Use the method of differences to find

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\frac{64 r^{3} + 16 r}{\left(2 r - 1\right)^{4} \left(2 r + 1\right)^{4}}\right)\]

in terms of \(n\).
parts.answer_html: \[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\frac{64 r^{3} + 16 r}{\left(2 r - 1\right)^{4} \left(2 r + 1\right)^{4}}\right)=\frac{8 n \left(n + 1\right) \left(2 n^{2} + 2 n + 1\right)}{\left(2 n + 1\right)^{4}}\]
parts.solution_html:
Use the following difference, obtained by combining the terms over a common denominator:

\[\frac{64 r^{3} + 16 r}{\left(2 r - 1\right)^{4} \left(2 r + 1\right)^{4}}=\frac{1}{\left(2 r - 1\right)^{4}}-\left(\frac{1}{\left(2 r + 1\right)^{4}}\right)\]

Writing \(F(r)=\frac{1}{\left(2 r - 1\right)^{4}}\) and denoting the requested finite sum by \(S_n\), the cancellation is

\[\begin{aligned}S_n&=[F(1)-F(2)]\\&\quad+[F(2)-F(3)]+\cdots\\&\quad+[F(n)-F(n + 1)].\end{aligned}\]

Only the first 1 and last 1 boundary terms remain (the formula also covers overlapping boundaries).

\[S_n=1-\left(\frac{1}{\left(2 n + 1\right)^{4}}\right)\]
\[S_n=\frac{8 n \left(n + 1\right) \left(2 n^{2} + 2 n + 1\right)}{\left(2 n + 1\right)^{4}}\]
parts.hint_html: Find a difference F(r)−F(r+h), then write the boundary terms before simplifying.

marking_points.criterion_html: Find an appropriate partial-fraction or difference representation.
Obtain the correct coefficients in that representation.
Display cancellation and retain every required boundary term.

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Determine whether the corresponding infinite series converges and, if it does, find its sum.
parts.solution_html:
The partial sums satisfy

\[S_n=\frac{8 n \left(n + 1\right) \left(2 n^{2} + 2 n + 1\right)}{\left(2 n + 1\right)^{4}}\]

Taking the limit as \(n\to\infty\) gives a finite number:

\[\lim_{n\to\infty}S_n=1\]

Therefore the series converges to this value.
parts.hint_html: Use the finite partial sum, not a sum of separate divergent series.

marking_points.criterion_html: Take the limit of the partial sum and justify the limiting boundary value(s).

parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html:
Use standard summation formulae to simplify

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 3\right) \left(r + 4\right)\right)\]

in terms of \(n\).
parts.solution_html:
Expand the summand and separate its powers of \(r\).

\[\left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 3\right) \left(r + 4\right)=r^{3} + 9 r^{2} + 26 r + 24\]

Use the standard formulae; the constant is counted once for each of the \(n\) terms.

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 3\right) \left(r + 4\right)\right)=1\left(\frac{n^{2} \left(n + 1\right)^{2}}{4}\right)+9\left(\frac{n \left(n + 1\right) \left(2 n + 1\right)}{6}\right)+26\left(\frac{n \left(n + 1\right)}{2}\right)+24\left(n\right)\]
\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 3\right) \left(r + 4\right)\right)=\frac{n \left(n + 7\right) \left(n^{2} + 7 n + 22\right)}{4}\]
parts.hint_html: Expand before applying the standard summation formulae.

marking_points.criterion_html: Expand and separate the polynomial into standard sums.
Apply the summation formulae with the correct limits and number of constant terms.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Express \(\frac{3 r + 8}{\left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 3\right) \left(r + 4\right)}\) in partial fractions. Hence find \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\frac{3 r + 8}{\left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 3\right) \left(r + 4\right)}\right)\).
parts.solution_html:
The simple partial fractions are

\[\frac{3 r + 8}{\left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 3\right) \left(r + 4\right)}=- \frac{2}{r + 4} + \frac{1}{r + 3} + \frac{1}{r + 2}\]

Use the following difference, obtained by combining the terms over a common denominator:

\[\frac{3 r + 8}{\left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 3\right) \left(r + 4\right)}=\frac{2}{r + 3} + \frac{1}{r + 2}-\left(\frac{2}{r + 4} + \frac{1}{r + 3}\right)\]

Writing \(F(r)=\frac{2}{r + 3} + \frac{1}{r + 2}\) and denoting the requested finite sum by \(S_n\), the cancellation is

\[\begin{aligned}S_n&=[F(1)-F(2)]\\&\quad+[F(2)-F(3)]+\cdots\\&\quad+[F(n)-F(n + 1)].\end{aligned}\]

Only the first 1 and last 1 boundary terms remain (the formula also covers overlapping boundaries).

\[S_n=\frac{5}{6}-\left(\frac{2}{n + 4} + \frac{1}{n + 3}\right)\]
\[S_n=\frac{n \left(5 n + 17\right)}{6 \left(n + 3\right) \left(n + 4\right)}\]
parts.hint_html: Find a difference F(r)−F(r+h), then write the boundary terms before simplifying.

marking_points.criterion_html: Find an appropriate partial-fraction or difference representation.
Obtain the correct coefficients in that representation.
Display cancellation and retain every required boundary term.

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Determine whether the corresponding infinite series converges and, if it does, find its sum.
parts.solution_html:
The partial sums satisfy

\[S_n=\frac{n \left(5 n + 17\right)}{6 \left(n + 3\right) \left(n + 4\right)}\]

Taking the limit as \(n\to\infty\) gives a finite number:

\[\lim_{n\to\infty}S_n=\frac{5}{6}\]

Therefore the series converges to this value.
parts.hint_html: Use the finite partial sum, not a sum of separate divergent series.

marking_points.criterion_html: Take the limit of the partial sum and justify the limiting boundary value(s).

parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: Show that the difference between the squares of \(2r+1\) and \(2r-1\) is \(8r\).
parts.solution_html: \[[(2r+1)-(2r-1)][(2r+1)+(2r-1)]=2\cdot4r=8r.\]
parts.hint_html: Use a difference of squares.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html:
Use the method of differences to find

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\frac{8 r}{\left(2 r - 1\right)^{2} \left(2 r + 1\right)^{2}}\right)\]

in terms of \(n\).
parts.solution_html:
Use the following difference, obtained by combining the terms over a common denominator:

\[\frac{8 r}{\left(2 r - 1\right)^{2} \left(2 r + 1\right)^{2}}=\frac{1}{\left(2 r - 1\right)^{2}}-\left(\frac{1}{\left(2 r + 1\right)^{2}}\right)\]

Writing \(F(r)=\frac{1}{\left(2 r - 1\right)^{2}}\) and denoting the requested finite sum by \(S_n\), the cancellation is

\[\begin{aligned}S_n&=[F(1)-F(2)]\\&\quad+[F(2)-F(3)]+\cdots\\&\quad+[F(n)-F(n + 1)].\end{aligned}\]

Only the first 1 and last 1 boundary terms remain (the formula also covers overlapping boundaries).

\[S_n=1-\left(\frac{1}{\left(2 n + 1\right)^{2}}\right)\]
\[S_n=\frac{4 n \left(n + 1\right)}{\left(2 n + 1\right)^{2}}\]
parts.hint_html: Find a difference F(r)−F(r+h), then write the boundary terms before simplifying.

marking_points.criterion_html: Find an appropriate partial-fraction or difference representation.
Display cancellation and retain every required boundary term.

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Determine whether the corresponding infinite series converges and, if it does, find its sum.
parts.solution_html:
The partial sums satisfy

\[S_n=\frac{4 n \left(n + 1\right)}{\left(2 n + 1\right)^{2}}\]

Taking the limit as \(n\to\infty\) gives a finite number:

\[\lim_{n\to\infty}S_n=1\]

Therefore the series converges to this value.
parts.hint_html: Use the finite partial sum, not a sum of separate divergent series.
parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: Find \(S_{25}\) correct to 3 decimal places.
parts.solution_html:
The cancellation gives

\[S_n=\frac4{\sqrt5}-\frac{n+4}{\sqrt{n^2+4n+5}}.\]
\[S_{25}=\frac4{\sqrt5}-\frac{29}{\sqrt{730}}\approx 0.715516.\]

Rounding only at the final step gives \(0.716\).
parts.hint_html: Identify F(r)−F(r+1) before calculating 25 terms.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html:
Find the least \(n\) for which

\[S_n\gt \frac4{\sqrt5}-\frac{21}{20}.\]
parts.solution_html:
The inequality reduces to

\[\frac{n+4}{\sqrt{n^2+4n+5}}\lt \frac{21}{20}.\]

Put \(m=n+2\ge3\). Both sides are positive, so squaring is equivalent:

\[400(m+2)^2\lt 441(m^2+1)\iff41m^2-1600m-1159\gt 0.\]

The function \((m+2)/\sqrt{m^2+1}\) decreases for \(m\ge3\), since its derivative is \((1-2m)/(m^2+1)^{3/2}\lt 0\). At \(m=39\) the quadratic is −1198; at \(m=40\) it is 441. Thus the least allowed \(m\) is 40, giving \(n=38\).
parts.hint_html: Square only after noting positivity, and verify minimality at adjacent integers.

marking_points.criterion_html: Square and obtain the correct quadratic inequality.
Identify the first admissible m=40 using monotonicity or roots.

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html:
For \(z\gt 0\), prove that

\[\arctan(z+3)-\arctan z=\arctan\frac3{z^2+3z+1}.\]
parts.solution_html:
Let \(A=\arctan(z+3)\) and \(B=\arctan z\). The tangent difference formula gives

\[\tan(A-B)=\frac{(z+3)-z}{1+z(z+3)}=\frac3{z^2+3z+1}.\]

Since \(0\lt B\lt A\lt \pi/2\), the difference lies in \((0,\pi/2)\). Therefore the principal arctangent gives exactly \(A-B\), with no extra multiple of \(\pi\).
parts.hint_html: Establish the range of the angle difference, not only equality of tangents.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Hence find \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}\arctan\frac3{r^2+3r+1}\).
parts.solution_html: Replace each term by \(\arctan(r+3)-\arctan r\). Three terms remain at each end after cancellation, giving the stated answer.
parts.hint_html: This is a three-step difference, so retain three boundary angles.

marking_points.criterion_html: Use the identity from part (a) at integer indices.

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Deduce the sum to infinity, simplifying your answer.
parts.solution_html: Each upper arctangent tends to \(\pi/2\). Also \(\arctan1+\arctan2+\arctan3=\pi\): the first two angles have tangent −3 and their sum is in \((\pi/2,\pi)\), so their sum is \(\pi-\arctan3\). Thus the total is \(3\pi/2-\pi=\pi/2\).
parts.hint_html: Use the branch-correct identity arctan1+arctan2+arctan3=π.

marking_points.criterion_html: Obtain π/2 with a valid limiting argument.

parts.prompt_html: Find \(S_N=\sum_{r=1}^{N}u_r\).
parts.solution_html:
All logarithm arguments are positive on the stated domain. Split each term into two logarithms:

\[u_r=\ln(2+x^{r+1})-\ln(2+x^r).\]

Cancellation gives \(\ln(2+x^{N+1})-\ln(2+x)\).
parts.hint_html: Use differences of logarithms of successive terms.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Determine every allowed real \(x\) for which the infinite series converges, and give its sum in each case.
parts.answer_html:
\[-1\lt x\le1.\]

For \(-1\lt x\lt 1\), the sum is \(\ln[2/(2+x)]\). At \(x=1\) the sum is 0.
parts.solution_html:
If \(|x|\lt 1\), then \(x^{N+1}\to0\) and the sum is \(\ln[2/(2+x)]\). At \(x=1\) every summand is zero.

At \(x=-1\), partial sums alternate between 0 and \(\ln3\), so there is no limit. For \(x\gt 1\) the numerator inside the logarithm grows without bound, giving divergence to infinity.
parts.hint_html: Do not substitute x=1 into the formula derived from |x|<1.

marking_points.criterion_html: Give the correct open-interval result, including x=0.
Exclude x=−1 and x>1 with valid reasons.

parts.prompt_html:
Use the method of differences to find

\[\sum_{r=0}^{n - 1}\left(\frac{1}{\left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 6\right)}\right)\]

in terms of \(n\).
parts.solution_html:
Use the following difference, obtained by combining the terms over a common denominator:

\[\frac{1}{\left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 6\right)}=\frac{1}{4 r + 8}-\left(\frac{1}{4 r + 24}\right)\]

Writing \(F(r)=\frac{1}{4 r + 8}\) and denoting the requested finite sum by \(S_n\), the cancellation is

\[\begin{aligned}S_n&=[F(0)-F(4)]\\&\quad+[F(1)-F(5)]+\cdots\\&\quad+[F(n - 1)-F(n + 3)].\end{aligned}\]

Only the first 4 and last 4 boundary terms remain (the formula also covers overlapping boundaries).

\[S_n=\frac{1}{8}+\frac{1}{12}+\frac{1}{16}+\frac{1}{20}-\left(\frac{1}{4 n + 8}\right)-\left(\frac{1}{4 n + 12}\right)-\left(\frac{1}{4 n + 16}\right)-\left(\frac{1}{4 n + 20}\right)\]
\[S_n=\frac{n \left(77 n^{3} + 838 n^{2} + 2947 n + 3338\right)}{240 \left(n + 2\right) \left(n + 3\right) \left(n + 4\right) \left(n + 5\right)}\]
parts.hint_html: Find a difference F(r)−F(r+h), then write the boundary terms before simplifying.

marking_points.criterion_html: Find an appropriate partial-fraction or difference representation.
Obtain the correct coefficients in that representation.
Display cancellation and retain every required boundary term.

parts.prompt_html: Determine whether the corresponding infinite series converges and, if it does, find its sum.
parts.solution_html:
The partial sums satisfy

\[S_n=\frac{n \left(77 n^{3} + 838 n^{2} + 2947 n + 3338\right)}{240 \left(n + 2\right) \left(n + 3\right) \left(n + 4\right) \left(n + 5\right)}\]

Taking the limit as \(n\to\infty\) gives a finite number:

\[\lim_{n\to\infty}S_n=\frac{77}{240}\]

Therefore the series converges to this value.
parts.hint_html: Use the finite partial sum, not a sum of separate divergent series.

parts.prompt_html:
Use the method of differences to find

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\frac{6 r + 8}{\left(r + 1\right) \left(r + 2\right) \left(3 r + 2\right) \left(3 r + 5\right)}\right)\]

in terms of \(n\).
parts.solution_html:
Use the following difference, obtained by combining the terms over a common denominator:

\[\frac{6 r + 8}{\left(r + 1\right) \left(r + 2\right) \left(3 r + 2\right) \left(3 r + 5\right)}=\frac{1}{\left(r + 1\right) \left(3 r + 2\right)}-\left(\frac{1}{\left(r + 2\right) \left(3 r + 5\right)}\right)\]

Writing \(F(r)=\frac{1}{\left(r + 1\right) \left(3 r + 2\right)}\) and denoting the requested finite sum by \(S_n\), the cancellation is

\[\begin{aligned}S_n&=[F(1)-F(2)]\\&\quad+[F(2)-F(3)]+\cdots\\&\quad+[F(n)-F(n + 1)].\end{aligned}\]

Only the first 1 and last 1 boundary terms remain (the formula also covers overlapping boundaries).

\[S_n=\frac{1}{10}-\left(\frac{1}{\left(n + 2\right) \left(3 n + 5\right)}\right)\]
\[S_n=\frac{n \left(3 n + 11\right)}{10 \left(n + 2\right) \left(3 n + 5\right)}\]

parts.prompt_html:
Use the identity

\[\sin[(2r+1)\theta]-\sin[(2r-1)\theta]=2\sin\theta\cos(2r\theta)\]

to find \(\sum_{r=1}^{N}\cos(2r\theta)\), where \(\theta\) is not an integer multiple of \(\pi\).
parts.solution_html:
Sum the identity over \(r=1,\ldots,N\). Every internal sine cancels, giving

\[2\sin\theta\sum_{r=1}^{N}\cos(2r\theta)=\sin[(2N+1)\theta]-\sin\theta.\]

Division by \(2\sin\theta\) is valid because \(\theta\notin\pi\mathbb Z\).
parts.hint_html: The restriction on θ is needed before dividing by sinθ.

marking_points.criterion_html: Sum the identity over the stated range.
Divide by 2 sinθ and state the formula.

parts.prompt_html: Set \(\theta=\pi/4\). Show that the infinite cosine series does not converge.
parts.solution_html:
Its terms repeat \(0,-1,0,1\). Consequently,

\[S_{4m}=0,\qquad S_{4m+2}=-1.\]

These two subsequences have different limits, so the partial sums do not converge.
parts.hint_html: Use two subsequences of partial sums, rather than relying on the word “oscillates”.

marking_points.criterion_html: Exhibit distinct partial-sum subsequences or a nonzero subsequence of terms.
